turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Tuesday, September 22nd. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex — and we're starting with a market surprise dressed up as a geopolitics story: oil just fell off a cliff because the Iran ceasefire is actually holding.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: WTI dropped 4.69% to $95.59 a barrel, Brent down 3.67% to $100.06 — that's the ceasefire hitting its ninth-plus day with real Trump-Tehran talks progressing, not just a pause holding by accident.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And that's separate from the bigger diplomatic story this week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Completely separate track — the UN General Assembly's 81st session opened in New York, roughly 130 world leaders in town, and it's Secretary-General Guterres's final high-level week before his term ends this year. Theme's "Restoring trust, managing transformation."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Who's actually meeting who?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Trump addresses the assembly today, under 40% approval domestically, framing himself as the peacemaker — first formal meeting with UK's new PM Andy Burnham, who replaced Starmer back in July, and with Japan's Takaichi. But the meeting to watch is an informal pull-aside with Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: First contact since the operation that captured Maduro.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly — and it follows the US-Venezuela oil deal from August and September that gave the Pentagon a 35% stake in a venture holding hundred-year rights to seventeen oil fields, 65 billion barrels of reserves. Guterres, meanwhile, is pushing separately for Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb navigation de-escalation and a Ukraine ceasefire.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second world story is grim — Bangladesh's measles outbreak just crossed a thousand child deaths.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 1,009 deaths since March, roughly 190,000 infected — the CDC is calling it the largest current measles outbreak anywhere in the world. WHO and UNICEF trace it to immunization-program gaps from the 2024-25 political turmoil, the procurement disruption after Hasina's ouster.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is the vaccination effort catching up at all?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: About 20 million doses given since April, but 4 million children are still missed — and Bangladesh is restarting a nationwide re-vaccination campaign this Thursday, the 25th. It's a genuinely global public-health story hiding behind a domestic political collapse.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Onto US business — and there's a merger that's finally allowed to close.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Paramount Skydance's $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. Discovery cleared its last real hurdle: a settlement with twelve Democratic state attorneys general, led by California's Bonta.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What did Paramount have to give up to get there?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: $300 million a year in additional US film production for five years — $1.5 billion total — plus a commitment to 30 films a year for two years, then 32 a year for three, with a $30 million penalty per shortfall film. A five-year ban on selling or closing the Paramount or Warner Bros. studio lots. $47.5 million into a worker-impact fund. And a new independent board specifically overseeing CBS News and CNN's editorial independence.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the piece that actually unlocks the deal — different from the bond-fight delay we covered before.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, this is the antitrust resolution, not the financing dispute. There's also a separate WGA settlement barring CBS News writer layoffs for five years, plus $17.5 million into the union's health fund.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second US story — Google's ad-tech antitrust case just got decided, and it's not a breakup.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Judge Leonie Brinkema's 106-page remedies opinion, unsealed last week, rejected the DOJ's push to force Google to divest its AdX exchange and DFP ad server. Instead: behavioral remedies. Google has to loosen bundling restrictions across the ad-tech stack and operate under an antitrust compliance monitor for six years.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A monitor instead of a structural fix — that's a real trend today.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's the pattern running through basically everything we're covering this morning — institutions choosing oversight over surgery. We'll come back to that.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: International — UBS is picking a fight with its own regulator today.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: CEO Sergio Ermotti, speaking at Bank of America's Financials CEO Conference, says Switzerland's proposed "too-big-to-fail" rules — requiring full equity-backing of foreign subsidiaries — would force roughly $23 billion in fresh capital demands on UBS alone.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a timeline on this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Seven years to comply starting 2028 under the current framework, but Swiss senators just delayed a vote over disputes on that foreign-subsidiary requirement specifically. Ermotti's floating AT1 bonds — contingent convertible debt — as a partial, "bearable" compromise instead of pure equity.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second international story — actually good economic news, with an asterisk.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Eurozone flash composite PMI hit 51.2 in September, a 16-month high — ninth straight month of expansion, manufacturing output up for a seventh consecutive month, services expanding since February 2024.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Where's the asterisk?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: France, specifically flagged as a drag in the report — the early-September government shake-up, the Bayrou collapse into the Lecornu government, is disrupting company production plans on the ground. So the currency bloc as a whole is accelerating while its second-largest economy is the one visible weak spot inside that number.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is that divergence new, or has it been building for a while?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's been building — Germany and the smaller peripheral economies have been the ones carrying eurozone momentum for months now, and this print is the first time the report's language singles out France by name as the specific drag rather than a general soft patch across the bloc.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets actually had a real day yesterday, not a "check the app" one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Nasdaq closed at a record — 27,122.09, up 2.26%. Chip stocks did the heavy lifting: Intel up 12%, AMD up 10% and crossing a trillion-dollar market cap for the first time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the S&P?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 7,764.70, up 1.49% — technically just under our 1.5% bar for a "major move," but CNBC's calling it the best single day since early August, so it earns the mention. Dow and Russell were both just routine, up under a point — full levels are on the Markets tab.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: You opened the show with the oil move — walk through why that's actually the story under the story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Iran ceasefire holding into a ninth-plus day, with real diplomatic talks rather than just silence, is what's pulling WTI down 4.69% and Brent down 3.67% — that's a genuine risk-premium unwind, not noise. Combine a collapsing geopolitical risk premium with an AI-chip earnings tailwind and you get a market that's re-pricing two separate fears downward on the same day.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does that risk-on move show up in rates and gold too?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 10-year Treasury eased about 4 basis points, still elevated but off last week's 19-year high near 5.04%. Gold actually dipped slightly, down about half a percent — which is the tell that this is a genuine risk-off unwind, not a flight to safety. When gold falls while equities rally on a de-escalation headline, that's the market believing the de-escalation, not hedging against it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything that should worry someone holding this rally?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The obvious one — ceasefires in that region have broken before, and a nine-day hold is encouraging but not proof of durability. The AI-chip leg of the rally is also getting concentrated in a small number of names, which is the same fragility we've flagged before: it's a powerful rally, but a narrow one underneath the index-level number.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Today's deep dive isn't markets and it isn't energy — it's the most literal case of state capture I think either of us has read this year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Where's this from?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This week's Economist newsletter, pointing to a 1843 investigation published last Friday: "He was one of the world's most wanted men. So he bought a west African country."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Who's the subject?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Jos Leijdekkers — Dutch, 33, goes by "Bolle Jos," "Chubby Jos," and the alias "Omar Sheriff." Sentenced in absentia to 24 years in the Netherlands for trafficking roughly seven tonnes of cocaine and orchestrating a murder, another 10 years in Belgium for trafficking and assault. On the Dutch national most-wanted list and the EU most-wanted list since May 2022.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And he's just — living freely somewhere?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: In Sierra Leone, since late 2022, under the "Omar Sheriff" identity, presenting himself as a Turkish investor. 1843's reporting says he did this with little more than a smartphone and a supplier network — and over about four years, embedded himself directly into Sierra Leone's political class.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does "embedded" actually mean here — bribery, or something more?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: More than bribery. By November 2024 he was engaged to Agnes Bio, daughter of President Julius Maada Bio — reports say they have a child together. January 1st this year, he's caught on video sitting beside Agnes Bio at a New Year's church service with the country's top officials present, completely unbothered.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The Netherlands has an extradition request in, presumably.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Filed, and going nowhere. And here's the part that turns this from a scandal into something structural — journalists in Sierra Leone investigating him face harassment, raids, and arrest. That's not incidental risk, that's the silence being actively maintained, not just tolerated.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there any external pressure building?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The EU is weighing cutting aid to Sierra Leone specifically over this. But think about what that lever actually is — foreign aid is the blunt instrument being reached for because the domestic instruments, law enforcement, extradition cooperation, a free press, have all individually stopped functioning around this one man.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Tie this back to the Google and Paramount stories from headlines.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly the connective tissue for the whole show today. Google gets a six-year compliance monitor instead of a breakup. Paramount-WBD gets an independent editorial board bolted onto the merger instead of a block. Both of those are functioning institutions choosing supervision over surgery. Sierra Leone is the other end of that same spectrum — a state where the supervision itself has been purchased, so there's no monitor left to bolt on.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a version of this where Sierra Leone's institutions actually recover?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The honest read is it depends entirely on outside pressure now, because the internal mechanisms — the press, the judiciary's willingness to pursue extradition — are exactly the parts that got captured first. When the referee is the first thing purchased, reform from inside becomes structurally very hard, which is precisely why 1843 built this piece around him specifically rather than around a policy or an institution in the abstract.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A genuinely different kind of story for us to run this deep on.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Worth it — because it's the plainest possible illustration of what "no oversight" actually looks like in practice, not in theory.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy — and there's a genuinely sharp new argument this week about why clean buildout keeps losing to gas behind the meter.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This is David Riester, of Segue Sustainable Infrastructure, in DealFlow.energy's newsletter — a piece called "The Last 10%." His thesis: solar-plus-storage covers about 90% of a large load's annual energy cheaply and fast. Batteries solve the diurnal problem well.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So what breaks past 90%?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pushing 90 to 95% roughly doubles the plan's cost. 95 to 100 is a further multiple on top of that — because the remaining hours aren't scattered randomly, they're clustered and correlated, a run of overcast January days when the whole system is short at once, not just one site.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why doesn't the load-serving entity just sell that last 10% as a product?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's Riester's actual point — there's no standard tariffed product for it. No LSE wants to stand behind 500 megawatts of new load while only selling the hardest 50 megawatts at a normal industrial rate. So the hyperscaler, wanting certainty, just builds the entire load itself behind the meter, sized for the worst 25 to 50 hours of the year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which means the gas plant ends up the same size as the data center.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Same nameplate capacity — roughly ten times what the actual energy gap required — running at a capacity factor that would embarrass a peaker plant, and contributing nothing to anyone else's reliability because it's fenced off behind that one meter. Multiply that by a few hundred campuses and that's the current buildout, in miniature.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's his actual fix?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A residual-firming tariff. Once a load demonstrably secures at least 80% of its annual energy from deliverable resources under defined performance criteria, it can buy firming for the rest at an openly-priced, resource-neutral, tariffed premium — storage of any duration, demand response, imports, or the utility's existing fleet. Gas only if it's genuinely cheapest, but visible and tariffed at 10% scale, not hidden behind a fence at 100% scale.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does this need new legislation?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: No new statute — FERC's pending large-load interconnection dockets are the natural vehicle, with states and PUCs holding the LSEs to actually naming and honoring that price. It's a market-completion argument, not a subsidy argument — his framing is that the obligation being created is simply the obligation to quote a price for a service the grid can already physically provide.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Any live data points backing up the urgency here?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Utility Dive's most-read story this week — a Pennsylvania PUC-commissioned study modeling PJM's 2030 reliability risk if data-center load growth continues. Worst case, the modeled loss-of-load expectation comes in over 100 times worse than PJM's own planning criterion — more than 13 days a year with loss-of-load events, against a one-day-in-ten-years standard.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a sharper number than the backstop-procurement story we've already covered.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely sharper, because it's a specific modeled figure from a state regulator, not a general warning — it's the PJM reliability story advancing with real math behind it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What happened in the deal market this week?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Thirteen deals, $39 billion, 3.5 gigawatts total. Biggest: AES Corporation's $33.4 billion take-private, PUCO approved the Ohio piece last Wednesday, buyers Global Infrastructure Management and EQT Infrastructure. Crusoe closed a $3.9 billion Series F, oversubscribed, $30.9 billion post-money — vertically-integrated AI infrastructure. And Jupiter Power landed $1.4 billion across ten utility-scale battery storage projects in Texas, 1.5 gigawatts, lenders including HSBC, SMBC, and MUFG.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That Jupiter deal is a lot of lenders for one portfolio.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Six different banks spreading exposure across ten separate project-level facilities — that's the financing market pricing battery storage as bankable at real scale now, not experimental.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does the Crusoe raise tell us anything about where AI-infrastructure capital is actually flowing right now?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It tells you vertically-integrated players — the ones that own generation, the data center, and the compute stack together instead of stitching separate contracts — are the ones pulling in the biggest single checks. A $30.9 billion post-money valuation for a company built specifically around owning its own power supply is the market voting that energy access, not chip access, is becoming the real bottleneck worth paying up for.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bago tayo pumunta sa Pilipinas, dalawang salita — parehas may kinalaman sa mga balitang pampulitika at pangnegosyo ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Simulan natin sa "pahayag."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Pahayag" — ang ibig sabihin, isang pormal na deklarasyon o pagbibigay-alam, karaniwang tungkol sa isang bagay na dati'y hindi pa lantad o kinukumpirma. Ginagamit ito kapag may nagsalita nang tuwiran tungkol sa isang usapin na dati'y basta tsismis o haka-haka lamang.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May kaibhan ba ito sa "pahayag" at, sabihin nating, "komento"?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Malaking pagkakaiba — ang "komento" ay pananaw o reaksyon lamang sa isang balita. Ang "pahayag" naman ay mismong ang bagong impormasyon mismo — ito na ang balita, hindi lamang reaksyon dito. Kaya kapag sinabing "opisyal na pahayag," ibig sabihin, seryoso at may bigat ang sinabi.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Ang pahayag ng alkalde ang nagbunyag ng koneksyon na dati'y itinatanggi ng lahat." Literal itong nangyari kanina lang, gagamitin natin ito sa susunod na segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sige, susunod — "pagsang-ayon."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Pagsang-ayon" — ang pagbibigay ng pahintulot o pagkakaunawaan sa isang panukala, karaniwang matapos ang mahabang pag-uusap o negosasyon. Ipinapahiwatig nito na dalawang panig na dati'y magkaiba ang tindig ay unti-unti nang nagkakaisa.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ano'ng pagkakaiba nito sa "usapan"?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang "usapan" ay maaaring impormal lamang — isang pag-uusap na hindi pa tapos o hindi pa opisyal. Ang "pagsang-ayon" ay ang senyales na malapit nang magkaisa ang dalawang panig — hindi pa ito ang pinal na kasulatan, kundi ang hudyat na malapit na ito.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Gamitin natin sa halimbawa.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Malapit nang magkaroon ng pagsang-ayon ang Pilipinas at Canada matapos ang buwan-buwang negosasyon." Gagamitin din natin ito mamaya.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May pagkakatulad ba ang dalawang salita bukod sa parehong balita?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo — pareho silang tungkol sa paglipat mula sa hindi tiyak patungo sa tiyak: ang "pahayag" ay naglalantad ng katotohanang dati'y natatago, at ang "pagsang-ayon" ay senyales ng papalapit na pagkakaunawaan sa isang usaping dati'y bukas pa. Dalawang paraan ng pagbabawas ng puwang sa impormasyon, isa sa pulitika, isa sa negosyo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ngayong araw, may bagong pahayag sa paglilitis kay Bise Presidente Sara Duterte — at galing pa mismo sa sarili niyang kapatid.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sino ang nagbigay ng pahayag?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Si Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte, kumpirmadong pumasok ang GenCorp Industries — kumpanyang may hawak si Sara Duterte simula 2013 — sa 19 na kontrata mula sa Davao City Hall, may halagang 33.26 milyong piso simula 2022.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English — that's a revised-up figure, from an earlier 14.32 million peso estimate, and Baste maintains he and city officials had no idea Sara held an interest in GenCorp, which is constitutionally barred while she's in office.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang tugon ng prosecution panel: tinawag nilang "confession of sins" ang pahayag ni Baste, at sinabing "tantamount to a smoking gun" — dahil sinisira nito mismo ang depensa ng Bise Presidente. Magte-testify mismo si Baste sa Setyembre 28 hanggang 30.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's also SEC testimony moving on a separate track — what's new there?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A SEC official testified Sara Duterte retained her GenCorp and family-company holdings even after her 2022 election, despite the constitutional prohibition. Separately, prosecution witness Gerardo del Rosario continued testimony that eight of Duterte's businesses filed no audited financial statements with the SEC at all — that's the unexplained-wealth thread of the impeachment case.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What about Romualdez — any movement there?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: One-line update: Sandiganbayan evidence pre-marking resumed today after a brief suspension over a traffic advisory, running through Thursday. Procedural, not a new angle — the real story stays the Duterte trial this week.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Onto the economic side — may pagsang-ayon bang malapit nang mangyari?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo — malapit nang magkaroon ng pagsang-ayon ang Pilipinas at Canada matapos ang ikaapat na round ng negosasyon noong Setyembre 8 hanggang 11 sa Toronto.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English — Trade Undersecretary Allan Gepty says there are "very few remaining issues" left, mainly agricultural market-access terms and the depth of implementation commitments, to be closed through smaller online sessions rather than another full negotiating round. Target's to conclude by November.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the data side — no active PAGASA storm signal today, just a low-pressure area far out east that might develop into a tropical depression, too distant to flag yet. And the PSEi's move was routine, down 0.21%, not worth a line beyond that.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, both built directly for the China story coming up — a new mechanism, and the reason for building it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First word: 机制, jīzhì — "mechanism." An abstract noun, formal register, used constantly in policy and diplomacy writing for a structured process or system, not a physical device.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does it typically pair with?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 建立机制, "to establish a mechanism," or 通知机制, "a notification mechanism" — which is exactly the phrase in today's story. It's distinct from 制度, which leans toward a formal institution or system of rules; 机制 is more about the actual working process underneath.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Example: 双方同意建立一个新的通知机制，以应对未来的危机。("Both sides agreed to establish a new notification mechanism to respond to future crises.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word — 以便, yǐbiàn.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: An HSK-4 connective meaning "so that" or "in order that" — it introduces the purpose or intended result of an action just described, and it's more formal than the everyday 为了, which usually comes before the action instead of after it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does the word order actually work?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Action first, then 以便, then the purpose — the opposite structure from 为了, which usually opens the sentence. 以便 signals "here's the outcome we're setting up for," almost like "in order to enable."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Example: 两国官员提前交换信息，以便在危机发生前采取行动。("Officials from both countries are exchanging information in advance, so that they can act before a crisis happens.") We'll hear both of these again in a moment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 双方同意建立一个新的通知机制，以便在人工智能事件升级为国安问题之前及时沟通。("Both sides agreed to establish a new notification mechanism, so that they can communicate in time before an AI incident escalates into a national-security issue.") That's not hypothetical — it's what Treasury Secretary Bessent and Vice Premier He Lifeng actually proposed this weekend.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Where did those talks happen?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: New York, concluding Sunday — Bessent's framing was "moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and number two AI powers." China hasn't publicly accepted the mechanism yet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's notably off the table?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: USTR Jamieson Greer confirmed chip and semiconductor export controls are not part of this specific track — this is narrowly an incident-notification proposal, not a broader trade or tech-restriction negotiation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: This is clearly setting up something bigger.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's the preview for the Trump-Xi summit in Washington this Thursday — Xi's first visit to Washington in a decade, the second Trump-Xi meeting this year after the May Beijing summit. Agenda covers trade, Taiwan, rare earths, and AI.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why propose an AI-safety mechanism specifically ahead of a summit about trade and Taiwan?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's the lowest-risk deliverable available — neither side has to concede anything on tariffs or sovereignty to agree to talk to each other before an AI incident spirals. It lets both leaders walk into Thursday with at least one thing to point to as a "de-escalation win," even if the harder issues stay exactly where they were.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does a notification mechanism actually constrain anything, or is it just diplomatic theater?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely somewhere in between — it doesn't restrict either country's AI development, but a standing communication channel for national-security-level incidents is a real, if narrow, guardrail. The test is whether China actually signs on by Thursday, or whether it just becomes one more thing "under discussion" that never quite closes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts today — the Booker Prize shortlist we previewed yesterday actually drops tonight.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 7pm British time, live at the Southbank Centre's Queen Elizabeth Hall in London — six novels cut down from that stacked thirteen-book longlist, drawn from 163 eligible titles published between October last year and this September.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Who's judging?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Classicist and broadcaster Mary Beard chairs the panel, alongside poet Raymond Antrobus, musician Jarvis Cocker, critic Rebecca Liu, and poet Patricia Lockwood — in conversation on stage with Booker Foundation CEO Gaby Wood, livestreamed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the names in contention are the same three we flagged yesterday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Same three — Douglas Stuart's "John of John," Marlon James's "The Disappearers," Elizabeth Strout's "The Things We Never Say," her third Booker nomination — plus three debut novelists also on the longlist who could easily bump one of the returning winners off the shortlist entirely.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: When's the actual winner announced?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: November 9th, at Old Billingsgate in London. What's genuinely unusual this cycle is the size of the names already on the longlist before tonight's cut.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Talk through why that matters for how the judges are reading this year.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two former winners and a three-time nominee all surviving to the eve of the shortlist reveal is rare — it reads as judges willing to reward a body of work at the height of its powers rather than defaulting to discovery for its own sake. Whichever of the three actually survives tonight's cut tells us which way this year's committee is leaning: prestige and craft, or making room for the three debut novelists still in the mix.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Op-eds — and Erdoğan himself is arguing the UN Security Council veto should simply be abolished.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bloomberg Opinion, published today. His case: recent crises — pandemics, energy shocks, supply-chain breaks, regional wars — prove a system where five capitals hold permanent veto power is incompatible with today's actually multipolar world. His proposal: no permanent members at all, a Council elected by the General Assembly on fixed, rotating terms.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a coherent diagnosis — the veto has repeatedly frozen the Council exactly when action was most needed, Syria and Ukraine both being live examples, and a rotating elected body would at least make blockage a matter of shifting coalitions rather than five permanent vetoes baked in forever.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The tell is who's making the argument — a Turkish president pitching veto abolition is a power seeking more influence dressed up as a power seeking less. Abolition without the P5's own buy-in is a non-starter, since they'd simply refuse to ratify it, and removing the veto could paralyze the Council further by replacing stable deterrence between great powers with shifting ad hoc majorities that are just as capable of freezing action, only less predictably.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second piece — Mihir Sharma at Bloomberg Opinion, and this one's about a movie.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A two-part de Gaulle biopic, based on Julian Jackson's 2018 biography, has become a genuine sensation in France — over 5.5 million viewers. Sharma's argument: the sovereignty-obsessed, America-distrusting de Gaulle feels newly vindicated to French audiences, and that nostalgia is France retreating into national myth instead of confronting its fiscal and political paralysis after the Bayrou government's collapse.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman that one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's something real in it — comfort-nostalgia for a strongman-unifier figure is a recognizable symptom when a country's political center can't hold, and France genuinely has been through three governments in barely a year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter-take?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Reading a box-office hit as proof of national "denial" stretches correlation into causation — France's fiscal debate is happening in parliament on its own timeline regardless of what's playing in cinemas, and audiences can enjoy a well-made historical epic without it being a referendum on their appetite for economic reform.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which lands harder this week?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Erdoğan piece, honestly — because whatever you think of the messenger, it's forcing an actual argument about institutional design, where the Sharma piece is closer to cultural commentary dressed up as economic diagnosis.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: We'll close today in Houston, with a Marine veteran named Mark Ackley.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's his story?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ackley beat Stage 3 lymphoma — and then, during chemo recovery, a serious back injury left him on a walker, facing the real possibility of a wheelchair.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a second fight stacked right on top of the first.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right on top of it — no break in between. A fellow Navy veteran, a rehab coach named Fenix Shepard, built him a slow, deliberate recovery plan from there, nothing rushed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Where did that plan actually lead?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: To a 90-day goal Ackley set for himself: scuba diving again, in full gear, roughly 60 pounds of it. He hit that goal.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Clean arc, no caveat needed there either.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: None — beat the cancer, beat the walker, and got back in the water on his own timeline, not anyone else's.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Tuesday, September 22nd.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Have a good one — we'll see you tomorrow.
